title: Operational Intelligence Is the New Control Plane
dek: Why enterprises need systems that reason across signals, workflows, people, and outcomes.
body: Every serious incident opens with the same twenty minutes, and almost none of it is spent on the problem. It is spent assembling: which services this transaction actually crossed, who owns the third one, what changed upstream in the last six hours, whether the component that looks broken was already degraded yesterday. Six engineers, six consoles, and a shared document that is stale before the call ends. The information was not missing. All of it existed, in a system somebody owned. It had simply never been assembled, and so it had to be assembled again, by hand, under time pressure, by people who would not remember the details next quarter.

That assembly is paid for on every investigation, by every engineer, every workflow, and now every agent. Each one reconstructs the same operational reality independently, pulling separately from a configuration database, an observability platform, an identity system, a ticket queue, a deployment pipeline and a topology store that do not agree with one another about what a service is. This is the Context Acquisition Tax. It is one of the largest recurring costs in enterprise operations and almost nobody carries it as a line item, because it is never billed in one place. It is billed twenty minutes at a time, forever.

Dashboards do not reduce that tax. They are one of the things being assembled. A dashboard answers whether a metric is inside a threshold, and it is genuinely good at that. What it cannot answer is which customer journey is affected, which dependency path explains the blast radius, what changed upstream, and what a human should approve — because answering those requires joining data that lives in six systems with six different models of the world. Adding a seventh dashboard does not close that gap. It widens it by one more thing to reconcile.

The distinction worth holding onto is this. Observability makes systems visible. Operational Intelligence makes operational meaning inspectable. Visibility is a precondition for the second, and it is not the same as understanding. I spent fifteen years watching telemetry volume rise far faster than operational understanding did: more instrumentation, better instrumentation, richer traces, and steadily less clarity per unit of data. That is not an argument against instrumentation. It is evidence that instrumentation was never the binding constraint.

For most of those years this was expensive but survivable, because a human did the assembly. Humans are slow at it and inconsistent at it, but they carry one property that turns out to matter more than speed: they know when they are guessing. An engineer working from a stale dependency diagram hesitates. They say the diagram is old. They go and check. The uncertainty is legible to everyone on the call, and the call slows down accordingly.

Production AI removed that property. A model asked to explain a live production system will produce a fluent, well-organized, confident explanation whether or not the context underneath it was complete. There is no visible difference between an answer grounded in current topology and one grounded in a snapshot that went stale three deploys ago. Both read like competence. Both arrive in the same shape, at the same length, with the same tone. That is an Authorized Misfire: the system did exactly what it was permitted to do, over context nobody had verified, and the output carried no signal that anything was wrong.

This is what moves the context layer from an efficiency project to a safety requirement. When humans did the reasoning, thin context produced visible hesitation. When a model does it, thin context produces prose. The failure stopped announcing itself, which means it now has to be engineered against rather than noticed.

So what does the layer actually have to hold? Transactions, so a signal can be tied to a journey somebody cares about. Topology, so blast radius is a fact rather than an assumption. Change, so correlation has a candidate cause to test. Ownership, so a recommendation has somebody to go to. History, so the last three occurrences of this pattern are available before anyone theorizes a fourth. Live telemetry, so none of the above is answered from memory. And provenance for every one of them.

Provenance is the piece dropped first and missed most. A fact without a source and a freshness stamp cannot be evaluated, only believed. In a system where a human reads every input, belief is survivable. In a system where a model consumes a thousand facts to produce one paragraph, belief is the whole vulnerability. Source and freshness have to travel with the fact, all the way to the conclusion, or the conclusion cannot be audited at all.

Calling this a control plane rather than a data platform is a deliberate claim about how it is operated. A data platform is filled and queried. A control plane is maintained continuously, consumed at decision time, governed like infrastructure, and treated as load-bearing — meaning somebody is accountable when it is wrong, and there is a defined way to find out that it is wrong. The point is one representation that humans, workflows, automation and agents all read, rather than each of them maintaining a private and slightly different copy.

The asymmetry underneath the whole argument is this: reasoning improves with every model release, for free, whether or not you do anything. Context improves only when somebody maintains it. Nothing in the industry's release cycle will hand you a better picture of your own estate. That is why the context layer, not the model, is the part worth owning — and why teams that start by choosing a model and end by discovering their topology data is unreliable have the sequence exactly backwards.

Four things have to be true of the layer for any of this to hold. Evidence comes before reasoning: current, attributable operational facts are assembled before a model is asked to explain anything. Freshness comes before confidence: historical memory can inform a decision, but it cannot stand in for current production truth. Evaluation and replay come before trust: reasoning that matters must be reproducible, contradiction-aware, and tested against regression rather than against a happy path. And human authority comes before consequential action: execution that is hard to reverse stays behind ownership, approval, and a path back.

None of these are model properties. All four are properties of the layer beneath the model, and all four can be built, tested and violated independently of which model is running that week. That is the practical reason to treat them as architecture rather than as guidance.

What this does not claim: Operational Intelligence does not eliminate dashboards, which remain the right tool for the question they answer. It does not replace the judgment of an experienced operator, and it is not an argument that incidents can be automated. It does not prove causality from sequence — a change that preceded a symptom is a candidate, not a cause, and a system that treats the two as equivalent is a faster way to be wrong.

What it does claim is narrower and, I think, harder to argue with: the decision path can be made inspectable, and once it is inspectable it becomes very difficult to fake. A conclusion that has to name its evidence, carry its provenance, show where confidence moved and why, state what it could not see, and stop at a named human is a conclusion that can be checked. Most operational AI cannot currently be checked at all. That is the gap worth building into, and it is a context problem long before it is a model problem.

title: Agentic Incident Investigation Without Losing Control
dek: How AI agents can accelerate enterprise investigations while keeping evidence, provenance, and accountability intact.
body: Incident investigation is a coordination problem wearing the costume of a search problem. It looks like finding something, so the instinct is to make finding faster. But the thing that makes a bad incident bad is rarely that the evidence was unavailable. It is that seven people held seven partial pictures, nobody held the whole one, and the group converged on the first explanation coherent enough to act on. Speed of retrieval was never the bottleneck. Coherence under uncertainty was.

This is why agents are genuinely promising here, and why the promise is so easy to squander. An agent is tireless in exactly the places humans degrade: it will check the fourteenth service as carefully as the first, it does not get invested in the hypothesis it proposed twenty minutes ago, and it does not stop looking because the shift ended. Those are real advantages and they compound at three in the morning.

The corresponding weakness is precise and it is not a lack of intelligence. A language model has no native representation of the difference between a fact it verified and a fact it inferred, and no instinct to stop when the evidence thins. Ask it to explain an incident with sixty percent of the relevant context and it will not return a sixty percent answer. It will return a whole one, in confident prose, with the gap seamlessly closed. Uncertainty gets compressed rather than reported, and compression is invisible in the output.

So the interesting design question is not how autonomous the agent should be. It is what has to exist around the agent so that its output can be checked. That surrounding structure is the harness, and the harness — not the model — is where the engineering lives. The harness owns scope, tool access, evidence capture, replay, evaluation, policy and human review. The agent is one component inside it, and a replaceable one.

The first thing the harness owns is typed evidence. Every fact entering the investigation is classified: observation, confirmed fact, contradiction, or unknown. Each one keeps its source and how fresh it is. This sounds bureaucratic until you watch what happens without it, which is that observations and inferences are stored in the same undifferentiated pile, and the model quite reasonably treats them as equally load-bearing. Untyped evidence is the mechanism by which a confident wrong answer gets built out of individually defensible parts.

The second thing is confidence that is permitted to fall. In OI-ROOM-001, the synthetic case this site uses throughout, the leading hypothesis reaches sixty-two percent as the transaction path is reconstructed and the evidence is typed. Then a healthy-looking metric turns up that is inconsistent with that hypothesis, a coverage gap is named, and confidence drops to thirty-eight. That fall is the most important number in the run. A confidence score that only ever rises is not a measurement, it is a presentation — and it is what you get by default, because every additional piece of evidence feels like progress.

The third is that contradictions are kept rather than resolved. The natural behavior of a summarizing system is to average conflicting signals into a coherent narrative, because coherence is what it was trained to produce. But the contradiction is precisely the point where an investigation should slow down, and it is precisely the point where an agent talks itself into an action. Keeping the contradiction visible, unresolved, and attached to the hypothesis it undermines is a design decision that costs fluency and buys safety.

The fourth is that a gap is reported as a finding. If the evidence does not cover a segment of the path, the system says so, in the output, as a first-class result. The alternative is inference across the gap, which is how a system produces an answer that reads well and is wrong in a way nobody can locate afterwards. Silence about coverage is not neutral. It is a claim of completeness that was never earned.

Only then do the gates make sense. Before anything is released to a human: is evidence coverage sufficient, can the run be replayed deterministically, did it stay inside its call budget, is the remaining uncertainty stated, does it respect confidentiality boundaries, has it been through review, and is the conclusion actionable at all. A failed gate stops the packet. Not warns about it — stops it. A gate that can be overridden by the thing it is gating is decoration.

And then the system stops. In OI-ROOM-001 the output is a rollback review packet that a named owner has to approve; the system recommends and cannot execute. This is the part most often argued about, and the argument usually assumes the constraint is about trust in the model. It is not. It is that the packet carries the evidence, the contradiction, the coverage gap and the confidence, so the person approving it decides with the same information the system had. Remove the human and you have not gained autonomy. You have removed the only component capable of noticing that the framing itself was wrong.

The failure modes are consistent and worth naming plainly, because each one is a specific engineering decision rather than a general risk. Over-broad tool access, where the agent can reach far more than the investigation requires. Hidden context, where something entered the prompt that never appears in the audit trail. Action without review. Stale topology, which produces confident reasoning over a system that no longer exists. Private memory leaking across boundaries it should not cross. And evaluations that test the happy path — the single most common one, because operational ambiguity is hard to write fixtures for and clean cases are easy.

What this does not claim: agents should not replace incident commanders, and the position that every incident can be automated is not one I hold or find plausible. Human judgment is doing something during an incident that is not search and not synthesis — it is deciding which question is worth asking next, under conditions the system was not designed for. Nothing here removes that.

What it does claim is a change in how these systems should be measured. Not by how autonomous the agent appears, which is a demo property and trivially gamed. By whether the system can prove what it used, what it ignored, what it inferred, what remains unknown, and what a human must approve before anything happens. An agent that cannot show its work should not be trusted with an operational decision, and an agent that can show its work turns out not to need much autonomy to be extremely useful.

title: Transaction Intelligence for Complex Enterprises
dek: Moving from isolated telemetry to transaction-aware explanations of customer and business impact.
body: A transaction is often the closest bridge between technical behavior and business meaning. When systems understand transaction paths, they can explain impact in the language of customers, operations, and revenue.
Transaction Intelligence combines traces, events, metadata, topology, and domain context. It gives AI systems a stronger unit of reasoning than individual logs or metrics.
The goal is not just faster troubleshooting. The goal is a shared operational memory that helps teams improve reliability, customer experience, and process quality.
Most enterprise systems are owned by technical boundaries, but customers experience journeys. Transaction Intelligence restores the journey as the unit of analysis.
A transaction-aware system can separate local noise from business impact. A service warning matters more when it sits on a critical path, repeats across journeys, or aligns with a recent change.
This is where knowledge graphs become practical. They connect transactions, dependencies, owners, known failure modes, and decisions into a form that AI can retrieve and reason over.

Executive summary: Transaction Intelligence is the missing layer because customers experience journeys, while teams often debug service boundaries. The transaction path is where technical evidence starts to carry business meaning.

Core thesis: a transaction-aware system can distinguish a local warning from journey degradation by asking whether the signal sits on a critical path, aligns with a symptom window, affects completion, or changes customer state.
Current limitation: telemetry is often indexed by component, not by the work the customer or business process is trying to complete. That makes AI retrieval noisy and RCA narratives brittle.
Proposed model: reconstruct hops, timestamps, identifier changes, state transitions, latency, failure points, missing evidence, and ownership across the journey before ranking hypotheses.
Operating implication: operators should review the journey before the RCA. A sequence alone is not causality, but it tells the system what evidence must be explained.
Failure modes: treating traces as complete truth, ignoring asynchronous work, losing identity across systems, and inferring business impact without transaction context.
Related framework layers: Signal, Transaction, Topology, Evidence, and Reasoning layers work together to convert observable symptoms into a reviewable explanation.

title: Evaluating AI for Operational Work
dek: A practical evaluation model for enterprise AI assistants that must be useful under uncertainty.
body: Operational AI should be evaluated against real work: investigation quality, evidence handling, refusal behavior, escalation judgment, latency, cost, and user trust.

A good evaluation set contains normal questions, ambiguous questions, confidential questions, missing-context questions, and adversarial prompts. The assistant must answer usefully without inventing authority.

The strongest systems pair offline evals with production feedback loops. They capture whether recommendations were used, corrected, ignored, or escalated, then improve the retrieval and reasoning system from that signal.
Operational evals should include failure cases, not only success cases. The assistant must be tested on vague prompts, missing data, stale context, sensitive requests, and pressure to guess.
The best metric is not whether the model sounds smart. It is whether the system improves a decision without hiding uncertainty.

A trustworthy assistant earns scope gradually. It starts by summarizing and retrieving. It earns the right to recommend only after evidence handling, refusal behavior, and escalation judgment are proven.
Executive summary: evaluation for AI-native operations is a control system, not a scorecard. It decides whether an answer, recommendation, or action path is grounded enough to move forward.

Core thesis: evals should test operational behavior: canonical definition accuracy, layer routing, citation presence, source validity, refusal quality, unknown handling, contradiction handling, and related-page navigation.
Current limitation: generic model benchmarks do not tell a platform team whether an incident assistant can handle missing context, confidential prompts, red herrings, or pressure to invent certainty.

Proposed model: pair deterministic fixtures with replay seeds. Each fixture defines expected behavior, evidence requirements, limitations, and the refusal boundary. Model-based grading can be added later, but the deterministic contract should be visible first.

Architecture implications: the eval harness needs access to approved public sources, retrieval output, expected answer shape, confidential-term checks, unsupported-claim checks, and regression history.
Failure modes: opaque aggregate scores, fixtures that only test easy success cases, evals disconnected from real product journeys, and metrics that imply trust without proving behavior.
What this does not claim: an eval gate cannot prove universal correctness. It narrows release risk by making expected behavior explicit and repeatable.

title: The Operational Intelligence Stack
dek: A reference model for moving from telemetry collection to enterprise explanation and improvement.
body: Operational Intelligence is a stack, not a feature. At the bottom are signals: metrics, logs, traces, events, changes, tickets, documents, and business process data. Above that is context: ownership, topology, transactions, risk, policy, and historical decisions.

The reasoning layer turns context into hypotheses, impact statements, and recommended actions. The control layer decides what can be automated, what needs review, what should be refused, and what must be escalated.
The highest-value layer is learning. Every investigation should improve the next one by adding approved memory, sharpening evaluation scenarios, and clarifying which recommendations actually helped.
The stack should be designed around provenance. Every answer should be able to point back to the approved source, signal, rule, or decision record that shaped it.
It should also be designed around boundaries. Some information can be summarized publicly, some can be retrieved only by specific roles, and some should never enter an assistant context.
When the stack is healthy, operations stops being a series of disconnected escalations and becomes a system that learns how the enterprise behaves.

title: Why Dashboards Are Not Intelligence
dek: Dashboards expose signals. Intelligence explains meaning, impact, confidence, and next action.
body: Dashboards are useful when the human already knows what to look for. They are weaker when the work is ambiguous, cross-system, time-sensitive, or politically complex. Most enterprise incidents fall into that second category.
Operational Intelligence does not replace observability. It makes observability more useful by connecting symptoms to transactions, topology, ownership, history, and business impact.
The question should move from 'which chart is red?' to 'what changed, what is affected, what evidence supports the hypothesis, and what should a responsible human do next?'
Dashboards are still necessary. They are just not sufficient. The next interface should preserve the raw signal while adding narrative discipline and decision context.
This is why observability and AI should be designed together. The AI layer cannot reason well if the telemetry layer lacks correlation, ownership, topology, and historical memory.

title: Incident Investigation as a Product Experience
dek: What changes when incident investigation is designed as a guided product, not a frantic search session.
body: Most incident workflows are stitched together during the incident. People jump between tools, chats, dashboards, tickets, and memory. That makes the investigation dependent on who happens to be present.

A product-quality investigation experience should guide the team through evidence collection, timeline construction, hypothesis ranking, confidence calibration, mitigation review, and post-incident learning.
AI is valuable when it reduces coordination cost while preserving judgment. The interface should make evidence visible, uncertainty explicit, and decisions reusable.
The product experience should feel like a guided investigation room. Evidence, timeline, hypotheses, impact, and recommended actions should be visible at the same time.
A good incident product avoids premature certainty. It lets the team compare explanations, mark what is unproven, and see which decision would be safest to review.
The final output should not be just an RCA paragraph. It should be a reusable record that improves future retrieval, future evals, and future team alignment.

title: Knowledge Graphs as Operational Memory
dek: Why enterprise AI needs relationships, not just documents, to reason about operations.
body: Retrieval over documents can answer many questions, but operational work depends on relationships. Services depend on other services, transactions cross boundaries, owners change, and incidents repeat through similar dependency paths.
A knowledge graph gives operational AI a structure for blast radius, ownership, transaction journeys, known failure modes, and decision history. It helps the system reason about why a signal matters.
The graph should stay public-safe or permission-aware. It should preserve provenance, avoid unapproved secrets, and make relationship freshness visible.
The practical test of a graph is whether it improves a decision. If it cannot explain impact, ownership, dependency risk, or known patterns, it is structure without operational value.
The best operational memory combines documents and relationships. Documents explain meaning. Graphs explain how things are connected.

title: AI Evaluation Is Operational Risk Management
dek: For enterprise operations, evals are not a lab exercise; they are how risk is controlled.
body: A generic model score does not tell an enterprise whether an assistant can handle a noisy incident, a confidential prompt, missing context, or pressure to overstate certainty.

Operational evals should include realistic scenarios, expected evidence behavior, refusal tests, escalation rules, retrieval checks, and human usefulness ratings. They should test how the system behaves when the right answer is 'I do not know.'
The best evaluation system becomes a feedback loop. Production corrections, ignored recommendations, accepted mitigations, and post-incident reviews all become signals for improving the assistant.
Risk management also means knowing what the assistant should refuse. A system that answers everything is not enterprise-ready; it is uncontrolled.
The eval suite should become a release gate. If groundedness, refusal, citation quality, or escalation judgment regresses, the assistant should not ship.

title: Agentic Systems Need Operating Models
dek: The hard part of enterprise agents is not autonomy; it is boundaries, ownership, and review.
body: An enterprise agent without an operating model becomes a clever interface to unclear authority. Before automation, teams need to define task scope, tool permissions, data boundaries, evidence requirements, and human approval points.
The useful pattern is bounded agency. Agents collect, correlate, summarize, compare, and draft. Humans approve actions that change systems, affect customers, or carry compliance risk.
The operating model should be inspectable. Every agent handoff should preserve task state, evidence, assumptions, and decisions so the next person or agent does not restart from zero.
Autonomy should be introduced by task class. Summarization, retrieval, and comparison are lower risk. System-changing actions require stronger controls, approvals, and rollback plans.
The lesson is simple: agentic systems need an operating model before they need more tools.

Executive summary: the Operational Intelligence Framework is that operating model. It turns enterprise AI from an answer generator into a controlled reasoning system with evidence, memory, evaluation, decision boundaries, and human accountability.
Core thesis: the ten layers are not decorative taxonomy. They are the minimum sequence needed to move from telemetry to a decision a human can inspect and challenge.

Problem statement: without a shared operating model, teams debate outputs instead of evidence. The system needs to show where a conclusion came from, which alternatives lost, and what remains unresolved.

Proposed model: Signal, Transaction, Topology, Evidence, Reasoning, Memory, Evaluation, Decision, Learning, and Operator layers form one loop. Each layer exists because a specific operational failure happens when it is skipped.

Public-safe example: OI-ROOM-001 begins as transaction degradation, becomes an evidence graph, moves hypotheses through confidence changes, creates a replay seed, passes evaluation gates, and ends at an operator approval boundary.
Tradeoff: the model adds structure and friction. That is intentional when the alternative is fast but unsupported operational certainty.
Revision date: 2026-07-16.

title: OI-ROOM-001 Control Comparison
dek: A public-safe field note for testing Operational Intelligence against dashboard-only, chatbot-only, and ticket-only investigation modes.
body: Executive summary: OI-ROOM-001 should not be treated as proof that Operational Intelligence is better because it looks more complete. It should be treated as a repeatable comparison protocol: give multiple investigation modes the same synthetic facts, red herrings, contradictory evidence, missing evidence, transaction timing, and approval boundary, then inspect what each mode preserves or loses.

The control question is simple: what evidence would convince an experienced SRE, platform architect, or AI governance reviewer that the model improves operational judgment rather than renaming existing incident practice? The answer cannot be a better-looking interface. It has to be a more reviewable decision path.

The shared case is public-safe and synthetic. A customer-facing transaction degrades after a recent change. Signals show latency movement, a dependency path, a misleading capacity clue, one contradictory evidence item, one missing evidence condition, a rollback review option, and a human approval requirement. Every comparison mode receives the same facts.

Dashboard-only mode should be judged on signal visibility, time-to-symptom, and operator synthesis burden. It will usually expose the red metrics quickly, but it can lose the transaction journey, the hypothesis state, the contradiction, and the missing-evidence condition unless a skilled operator reconstructs them manually.

Chatbot-only mode should be judged on explanation fluency, grounding, refusal behavior, and whether it names uncertainty. It may summarize the incident quickly, but it is weak if it compresses conflicting evidence into a confident RCA, cites no sources, or recommends action without approval context.

Ticket-only mode should be judged on coordination, durable record quality, and post-incident usefulness. It may preserve comments and owner decisions, but it is weak if the hypothesis lifecycle is implicit, the transaction timing is scattered, and the final resolution cannot be replayed from evidence.

Operational Intelligence mode should be judged on whether it separates observation, inference, contradiction, missing evidence, confirmed fact, hypothesis movement, evaluation gates, and operator approval. It succeeds only if a reviewer can see how evidence changed confidence and where the system refused to overstate certainty.

The scorecard should not collapse into one aggregate number. Reviewers should inspect seven dimensions: evidence completeness, transaction reconstruction, contradiction handling, missing-evidence honesty, hypothesis quality, decision safety, and replayability. A mode can win one dimension and lose another.

The expected advantage of Operational Intelligence is not speed alone. The expected advantage is reduced reasoning loss: fewer unsupported conclusions, clearer unknowns, better handoff, safer action review, and a reusable record for evaluation and memory.

The strongest falsification test is independent implementation. If two teams use the doctrine and produce incompatible decision packets for the same OI-ROOM-001 facts, the doctrine is underspecified. If dashboard-only or ticket-only workflows preserve the same reasoning quality with less structure, the Operational Intelligence layer should be simplified.

This field note is a measurement design, not a published benchmark result. It does not claim that Operational Intelligence has already outperformed the controls in production. It defines what must be measured before that claim would be credible.

The Evidence Pack now turns this protocol into a reviewer-run worksheet: same facts, four modes, evidence table, dimension-level verdicts, reviewer notes, and failure examples. The goal is to make the thesis harder to fake, not easier to market.

reviewWorksheet.title: Reviewer worksheet
reviewWorksheet.purpose: Use the same OI-ROOM-001 facts across four modes and record what each mode preserves, loses, or invents.

modes.preserves: Signal visibility and fast symptom detection.
modes.likelyLoss: Transaction journey, hypothesis state, contradiction, and missing evidence unless an operator reconstructs them manually.
modes.reviewerQuestion: Can the reviewer reproduce why the leading hypothesis changed?

modes.preserves: Fast narrative synthesis and exploratory question answering.
modes.likelyLoss: Source validity, contradiction handling, approval context, and refusal posture if the answer is not grounded.
modes.reviewerQuestion: Does the answer cite evidence and admit missing context before recommending action?

modes.preserves: Coordination record, ownership comments, resolution notes, and durable follow-up work.
modes.likelyLoss: Live hypothesis movement, transaction timing, and a replayable evidence chain.
modes.reviewerQuestion: Can a future team replay the decision without asking who was present?

modes.preserves: Observation, inference, confirmed fact, contradiction, missing evidence, evidence graph, hypothesis lifecycle, eval gates, approval class, and replay seed.
modes.likelyLoss: Adds structure and review friction; simplify the layer if it does not improve reasoning quality.
modes.reviewerQuestion: Does structure reduce reasoning loss enough to justify the workflow?

dimensions.ask: Are supporting, weakening, contradictory, and missing evidence visible?
dimensions.failureSignal: Only red metrics or prose summary remain.

dimensions.ask: Can the reviewer follow the affected journey and timing?
dimensions.failureSignal: Impact is inferred from a component alert alone.

dimensions.ask: Does weak evidence reduce confidence or redirect the hypothesis?
dimensions.failureSignal: Contradiction is omitted from the final answer.

dimensions.ask: Are unavailable facts preserved as unknowns?
Are alternatives compared with falsification criteria?
dimensions.failureSignal: The first plausible explanation becomes the RCA.

dimensions.ask: Is the action reversible, owned, and approval-gated?
dimensions.failureSignal: Action is recommended without owner review.

dimensions.ask: Can another reviewer reproduce the reasoning path?
dimensions.failureSignal: Outcome depends on a private conversation or memory.

falsification: Dashboard-only or ticket-only preserves the same reasoning quality with less structure.
Two independent teams produce incompatible decision packets from the same doctrine and facts.
The Operational Intelligence workflow hides uncertainty behind process language.
Reviewers cannot identify where confidence changed or why action was gated.
